claims.text: Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia ruled on August 5, 2024 [Source: ev-1], that Google is a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising, thereby violating Section 2 of the Sherman Act [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: The court found this monopoly was maintained through exclusionary conduct involving default-distribution deals, where Google paid companies such as Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions to be their default search engine [Source: ev-1].

Evidence indicated that Google’s CEO Sundar Pichai testified the company spent approximately $26.3 billion on distribution in 2021, and trial evidence showed Google paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1].
This practice created a self-reinforcing loop wherein defaults generated scale, which produced data, improved quality, and ultimately protected the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1].

On August 5, 2005 (noted as 2025 in the source text), Judge Mehta ordered structural remedies requiring Google to sell Chrome, marking the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000 [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: Additionally, Google is prohibited from paying for default search placement or entering into revenue-sharing agreements, and it faces limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].

Google appealed this decision to the DC Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025, arguing that the trial court punished procompetitive innovation, with the final outcome remaining pending through 2025 [Source: ev-1].
A US court found Google's search business a monopoly because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by engaging in exclusionary conduct through default-distribution deals [Source: ev-1].
